label: 8 Nov
title: Prefix sums, difference arrays, hashing
focus: Count subarrays by remembering earlier prefix values in a HashMap.
learn: P[i] = a[0] + … + a[i−1], so sum(l..r) = P[r+1] − P[l]. Use long.
Counting subarrays with sum k: at each index, count earlier prefixes equal to P − k. Seed the map with {0: 1}.
For "divisible by k", store Math.floorMod(P, k); Java's % can be negative.
Many range adds, read once: d[l] += v; d[r+1] −= v, then take a running sum.
infy: Q1 is often an array problem with a counting twist. Prefix sums + HashMap is one of the most reported Infosys patterns.

label: 10 Nov
title: Sorting and greedy: intervals
focus: Sort by the right key, then make one decision per element. Check the greedy by swapping two choices.
learn: Exchange argument: if swapping two neighbouring choices never helps, the sort order is optimal.
Most non-overlapping intervals: sort by END. Fewest platforms or rooms: the busiest moment, found with a sweep.
Comparators: Arrays.sort(a, (x, y) -> Integer.compare(x[1], y[1])), never x[1] − y[1].

infy: Q2 is often a greedy problem. Minimum platforms and Largest number are both on the most-reported Infosys list.

label: 11 Nov
title: Greedy with heaps
focus: Unlock options in sorted order, keep the unlocked ones in a heap, undo your worst choice when a limit breaks.
learn: "Best among the options unlocked so far": sort by the unlock key and push options into a PriorityQueue as they unlock.

label: 14 Nov
title: Bits and XOR
focus: Each bit is independent in a sum of XORs. A trie answers pair questions; a basis answers subset questions.
learn: x & −x is the lowest set bit; write 1L << k when k can reach 31.
Prefix XOR: xor(l..r) = P[r+1] ^ P[l], exactly like prefix sums.
Binary trie: walk from the top bit, choosing the opposite bit to maximise the XOR.
XOR basis: at most one number per highest bit; the maximum subset XOR is built greedily.
infy: There are two XOR repeats: "at most N/2 elements, max XOR" (13 reports) and "X ≤ K maximising Σ X xor A[i]" (6 reports). The sample Hard problem is XOR-based too.

label: 16 Nov
title: Number theory toolkit
focus: gcd, sieves, fast power, inverses, nCr, and the square-free kernel.
learn: lcm = a / gcd(a, b) * b: divide first so it doesn't overflow.
The smallest-prime-factor sieve factorises any x ≤ 10⁷ in O(log x).
Fermat inverse a^(MOD−2) when MOD is prime; precompute factorials for O(1) nCr. A non-prime modulus (Infosys has used 10000) needs Pascal's triangle.
x·y is a perfect square ⇔ kernel(x) = kernel(y), where the kernel keeps the primes with an odd exponent.
infy: The sample Easy (perfect-square products) and Medium (gcd exactly p) are both number theory at their core.

label: 25 Nov
title: Trees II: tree DP, rerooting, small-to-large
focus: dp[v][state] from the children, answers for every root in O(n), and merging the smaller set into the larger.
learn: Tree DP: a few states per node (taken / not taken), combined from the children.

Small-to-large: keep the bigger child set and pour the smaller sets into it. This is exactly the sample Easy problem.

label: 26 Nov
title: Fenwick trees and segment trees
focus: Point updates with range queries for sum, min and gcd, coordinate compression, and Euler tours.
learn: Fenwick: point add plus prefix sum. "Count smaller to the right": scan right to left over compressed values.

infy: The sample Medium is a gcd segment tree plus one counter. CF 914D (bonus) is the closest public problem to it.

label: 27 Nov
title: Lazy segment trees and the K-parts DP
focus: Range updates, then the split-into-K-parts DP that Infosys reuses for its hardest problems.
learn: Lazy propagation: store a pending add on a node and push it down before visiting its children.
K parts: dp[k][i] = best over j of dp[k−1][j] + cost(j, i−1). O(K·n²) gets the small tests.
When moving i changes cost by a range add over j (distinct counts do), keep dp + cost in a lazy segment tree.
infy: The Infosys "gift boxes" problem is CF 833B and "k segments, minimum cost" is CF 1527E, with the same limits. Both are today's bonus problems.

label: 28 Nov
title: Backtracking, bitmask DP, digit DP
focus: Brute force for partial marks, dp[mask] for n ≤ 20, and counting numbers digit by digit.
learn: Choose, recurse, un-choose. A bitmask loop enumerates every subset for n ≤ 20.
Bitmask DP: dp[mask] or dp[mask][last], masks in increasing order; 2²⁰·20 ≈ 2·10⁷.
Digit DP: state (position, tight, extra); answer for [L, R] = f(R) − f(L − 1).
infy: Reported recent hard problems include "tree + DP + backtracking + bitwise" and a bitmask-DP graph problem.
